kp.k: Function-level detection tracks AI usage beyond access and surveys
kp.d: Daniotti, Wachs, Feng and Neffke study software development, not legal services. Their dataset covers 31 million contributions and 5 million extracted Python functions from 2019–2024; the abstract reports 170,000 developers overall. US collection targets eligible public Python contributors, while other-country collection samples 2,000 programmers per country-year in China, France, Germany, India and Russia. The method measures inferred intensity of AI use rather than access to tools or self-reported adoption, retaining functions with modifications to over 80% of their lines.
qs: We apply this classifier to 5 million functions extracted from 31 million contributions to Python projects from the beginning of 2019 to the end of 2024
In contrast, our approach allows us to quantify the intensity with which the technology is used in real-world work activities.

kp.k: Detection uses synthetic training and misclassification corrections
kp.d: The authors fine-tune GraphCodeBERT with a classification layer on around 8,000 functions, combining human-written examples with synthetic counterparts generated through a two-LLM description-and-implementation procedure. They report out-of-sample ROC AUC of 0.96, average precision of 0.9685 and F1 of 0.8911 at a 0.5 threshold. Usage estimates are corrected using country-specific true- and false-positive parameters; Table S2 reports US values of 0.9550 and 0.2321 respectively. Corrected estimates and confidence intervals can extend below zero.
qs: The total size of the training set amounts to around 8,000 functions.
We can use this equation to correct the estimated AI adoption probabilities from our AI detector for miss-classification errors.

kp.k: Real-world and newer-model detection is less reliable
kp.d: WildChat validation reports average true-positive probabilities of 0.701 and 0.698 for first-round and later-round GPT-3.5-turbo outputs, and 0.675 and 0.651 for GPT-4. The authors interpret these as showing reduced real-world reliability but little sensitivity to interaction rounds. Before additional training, corresponding probabilities for DeepSeek-V3, Claude Sonnet 4, o3 and GPT-4.1 are 0.452, 0.630, 0.867 and 0.763; after retraining they become 0.561, 0.831, 0.910 and 0.781. Maintaining detector performance through future retraining is an expectation, not an established result.
qs: The detection model is still predictive, especially for the newer OpenAI models, but struggles in differentiating between human code and code generated by either Claude or DeepSeek.
We therefore expect that by expanding the training set, we may be able to maintain the detector’s performance also as genAI technologies improve, at least in the near future.

kp.k: AI diffusion is rapid but geographically uneven
kp.d: By the end of 2024, the estimated US AI-generated function share is approximately 29% (28.6% in calculations), compared with 23/24% for Germany and France and 20% for India. China and Russia lag. Growth spikes coincide with major releases, including Copilot, ChatGPT and subsequent LLMs. The authors describe a sustained but shrinking US lead and suggest provider access restrictions and censorship as possible explanations for lower Chinese and Russian uptake, rather than identifying these mechanisms causally.
qs: About 29% of Python functions in the US were generated by AI by the end of 2024, closely followed by 23/24% for Germany and France.
India draws close at 20%, after having initially lagged in adoption.
However, other major countries are quickly catching up, eroding the US’ first-mover advantage.

kp.k: Newer developers use AI more intensively
kp.d: For US developers in 2024, the authors report AI use in 37% of code from newly joined GitHub users versus 27% among the most experienced. Experience is proxied by GitHub tenure or recorded activity, not directly measured professional competence. They find no significant usage difference between men and women using name-based gender inference, while acknowledging that inferred gender may not match identity; primary comparisons use only confidently classified male and female names.
qs: whereas the most experienced developers use genAI in 27% of their code, programmers who have just joined the GitHub platform use these tools for 37% of code.
As a consequence, this gender may not accurately reflect the gender the user identifies with.

kp.k: AI usage is associated with modest output gains
kp.d: US user-quarter regressions compare changes within developers while controlling for user and quarter fixed effects, using one-quarter-lagged AI usage and user-clustered standard errors. The constructed panel includes 100,097 users observed for an average of 5.1 quarters; the baseline regressions report 123,428 observations. Moving from zero to the end-2024 US usage rate is associated with approximately 3.6% more quarterly commits. Positive coefficients also appear for multi-file commits and commits introducing imports, although Table S7 reports different coefficient magnitudes across these outcomes.
qs: Moving from 0 to 29% genAI usage—the estimated US adoption rate by the end of 2024—is associated with a 3.6% increase in commit rates across all these commit types.
our primary specification uses a one-quarter lagged measure of AI adoption.
This avoids mechanical relations between observed AI adoption and commit-based variables.

kp.k: Experienced developers capture the measured productivity benefits
kp.d: The authors classify developers with at least six years of GitHub activity as experienced. At 29% AI usage, their model implies a 6.2% increase in commit rates for this group, with no statistically significant effect among less experienced users. Productivity and exploration gains concentrate almost exclusively among experienced developers despite greater usage among newcomers. The authors interpret this as widening rather than closing the skill gap.
qs: We classify users with 6 or more years of activity on GitHub as experienced programmers, and those with less than 6 years as less experienced.
for whom a 29% adoption rate would imply a 6.2% increase in commit rates
In contrast, we observe no statistically significant effects among inexperienced users.
However, experienced programmers capture nearly all of these productivity and exploration gains, widening rather than closing the skill gap.

kp.k: AI is associated with exploration of new programming domains
kp.d: At average end-2024 US usage, models predict 2.7% more new library combinations. The authors treat libraries and combinations as proxies for functionality and technical exploration, interpreting the association as possible expansion into unfamiliar programming domains rather than directly measuring skill mastery. They test restrictions to the 5,000 most common libraries and aggregation into 124 categories to address irrelevant imports and small technical differences. Table S7 nevertheless shows that not every library-entry measure is statistically significant. Exploration gains, like output gains, concentrate among experienced developers.
qs: At average end-of-2024 AI use rates for US developers, our models predict that developers will implement 2.7% more new combinations of libraries.
Libraries, and especially combinations of libraries used by programmers, therefore provide a rough indication of what kind of program a user works on.
However, both productivity and exploration gains concentrate almost exclusively among more experienced developers.

kp.k: Causal interpretation remains limited despite robustness checks
kp.d: The authors explicitly acknowledge that their observational design is not optimized for causal identification. Pre-2022 placebo regressions find no statistically significant associations, but have weak statistical power. Measurement-error exercises produce larger coefficients as estimated noise declines, which the authors interpret as evidence of attenuation and conservative baseline estimates; the derivation assumes independent measurement error. Tests of nonlinearities offer insufficient precision to establish thresholds or flattening benefits.
qs: Despite controlling for observed and unobserved user characteristics, our estimation design is not optimized for identifying causal effects.
However, the imprecisely estimated point estimates show that the statistical power of these placebo tests is not very strong.
Across all models, as measurement error falls, effect estimates rise.
Although point estimates suggest there may be a threshold above which benefits of additional AI usage rates flatten off, the precision of these estimates is too low to warrant strong conclusions.

kp.k: Commit counts do not establish code quality
kp.d: The study measures online contribution activity, not quality-adjusted output, issue resolution, successful merges or test coverage. It excludes coworker spillovers and firm-level productivity heterogeneity. Generalization is limited by its focus on open-source Python, six countries and self-reported GitHub locations; China presents an additional selection concern because developers also use Gitee. Similarity to coding adoption figures reported by Microsoft and Amazon is offered by the authors as support for external validity, not direct validation across all software work.
qs: Within software, we focus only on Python-based open-source contributions.
More generally, we also do not account for potential externalities between coworkers or heterogeneity in productivity across firms
We therefore leave questions of the effect of genAI on code quality for future research.

kp.k: Economic valuations depend on substantial extrapolation assumptions
kp.d: Combining occupation-level task data, wages and Llama 3.3 estimates of programming task shares, the authors report annual US coding-related labor costs of $637–1,063 billion. Applying the baseline 3.6% commit association yields $23–38 billion in annual additional value only if Python findings generalize and more commits causally represent valuable output. A Python-only scenario is reported as approximately $4–6 billion in the discussion but $3.2–5.3 billion in the methods. These are back-of-the-envelope scenarios, not measured revenues, savings or GDP effects.
qs: we arrive at a total value of productivity increases in US coding work of between 23 and 38B USD a year.
including that more commits translate into more valuable code
This estimate treats productivity gains as similar across programming languages.

kp.k: Other studies imply different productivity and valuation ranges
kp.d: The authors distinguish their own associations from causal estimates reported in prior laboratory, field and natural experiments. Their discussion scales task-completion estimates to a 29% adoption rate, giving 6.0%–15.7% productivity gains and $38–167 billion in annual direct value. Methods report an average task-completion-based scenario of 9.7% and $62–103 billion, versus 2.35% and $15–25 billion using average commit and merged-pull-request effects. They propose measurement error and differences in studied populations as explanations for discrepancies, rather than treating these estimates as interchangeable.
qs: our estimates are generally smaller than those found in RCTs
The higher effect estimates in prior literature may therefore also reflect differences in the populations and complier samples they studied.
yields an 2.35% increase in productivity or 15B-25B USD in annual value.

kp.k: Lower code prices could redistribute productivity gains
kp.d: The authors model possible price and welfare consequences rather than measuring them. Greater code supply can lower prices, benefit consumers and stimulate demand while reducing suppliers’ returns. Polar scenarios of perfectly elastic versus perfectly inelastic supply yield different distributions of gains; producer effects are ambiguous under fixed supply. Methods give a $21–126 billion welfare range using the study’s baseline productivity estimates, depending on elasticity and market assumptions, and explicitly characterize the extreme supply assumptions as unrealistic.
qs: Because this yields cost savings for consumers of code, while reducing profits for suppliers (i.e. programmers), factoring in such general equilibrium effects further widens the range of possible outcomes
Consequently, the net effect on the producer surplus is ambiguous.
However, the upper bounds of these estimates refer to the extreme situation where supply of code is perfectly elastic.

kp.k: Longer-run benefits may require complementary organizational changes
kp.d: Drawing on general-purpose-technology history, the authors take an explicitly optimistic position on future productivity, arguing that workflow integration, training and complementary assets take time. They call for research on individual, firm, regional and national adoption barriers and on effects among elite programmers. They also report another study’s finding that AI access shifts elite developers from managerial tasks toward coding, identifying task-composition change as a possible productivity mechanism not established by their own programming-only analysis.
qs: it takes time to integrate them into firm level workflows and procedures, train individuals and amass the complementary assets needed to fully exploit their potential.
Based on this, we find ourselves on the bullish side of the debate when it comes to the productivity effects of genAI.
Additionally, these barriers need to be understood not only at the individual level, but also at the firm, regional, and national levels.
an important margin along which productivity effects materialize is shifts in the task composition of software developer jobs.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Daniotti, Wachs, Feng and Neffke claim that generative AI adoption in coding is rapid but geographically uneven, with a shrinking US lead.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study of software development, not legal services. The authors estimate that AI generated or substantially assisted approximately 29% of the studied US Python functions by the end of 2024, compared with roughly 23–24% in Germany and France and 20% in India. China and Russia lagged. These percentages concern the share of functions, not the percentage of developers adopting AI. The authors suggest that provider access restrictions and censorship may explain some geographic differences; they do not establish those explanations empirically.

pts.k: The authors associate AI use with increased coding output and exploration of new technical domains.
pts.d: Moving from zero AI use to the estimated end-of-2024 US usage rate is associated with approximately 3.6% more quarterly commits overall. At that usage rate, the models also predict 2.7% more new combinations of software libraries, which the authors interpret as experimentation and expansion into unfamiliar development domains. The authors sometimes describe these relationships causally, but explicitly qualify their identification strategy in the supplement. Library combinations are indicators of exploration, not direct demonstrations of acquired competence or successful innovation.

pts.k: The authors estimate that AI coding assistance could generate tens of billions of dollars in annual US value, conditional on substantial extrapolations.
pts.d: Their baseline calculation values additional annual code at $23–38 billion by applying the estimated 3.6% output gain to $637–1,063 billion in annual coding-related labor costs. This assumes end-of-2024 usage and productivity patterns generalize beyond open-source Python and that extra commits represent valuable code and causal labor-productivity gains. A Python-only scenario is much smaller: the main text reports approximately $4–6 billion, whereas the supplement reports $3.2–5.3 billion. Alternative calculations importing task-completion effects from cited experiments yield $38–167 billion. These are scenario calculations, not measured revenues, realized savings, or directly observed GDP gains.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The diffusion claims rest on classifier-estimated AI assistance in large-scale GitHub data; output claims rest on within-user panel regressions.
pts.d: The study covers approximately 170,000 developers, 31 million contributions and five million extracted Python functions from 2019–2024. It combines a broad US collection with samples of 2,000 programmers per country-year in five other countries. A GraphCodeBERT-based classifier trained on roughly 8,000 human and synthetically generated functions achieves an out-of-sample ROC AUC of 0.96. Country-specific corrections adjust detected shares for false positives and true positives. US output regressions use user and quarter fixed effects, one-quarter-lagged estimated AI usage, and user-clustered standard errors; the baseline table reports 123,428 observations. Robustness checks include pre-2022 placebos, alternative library measures, and measurement-error analyses. These are observational estimates rather than randomized treatment effects.

pts.k: Economic value estimates combine the study's own coding results with occupational data, LLM-estimated task shares, external experiments, and stylized market assumptions.
pts.d: The authors use O*NET task information, 2023 BLS and American Community Survey employment and wage data, assumptions translating task frequency into working-time shares, and Llama 3.3 estimates of programming intensity across roughly 900 occupations. The broader productivity scenarios draw on cited lab and field experiments, rather than the GitHub panel alone. The supplementary market calculations assume linear demand and polar cases of perfectly elastic or perfectly inelastic code supply. With no direct estimate of code-demand elasticity, they use patent and trademark studies as analogies. These assumptions produce illustrative welfare bounds rather than an empirically calibrated general-equilibrium forecast.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern public Python development through December 2024 and do not establish effects on code quality, all software work, or other professions.
pts.d: The study measures newly created or heavily modified functions, retaining functions with modifications to over 80% of lines. The 29% headline describes the end of 2024, notwithstanding the document's 2026 publication label. Scope limitations include Python-only open-source work, selected countries, possible Chinese sample distortion from use of Gitee, and unmeasured coworker spillovers and firm heterogeneity. Detection is less reliable on real-world interactions and some newer models. The authors argue that measurement error likely makes their output estimates conservative, conditional on their measurement-error assumptions. They leave code quality for future research, so increased commits are not directly demonstrated quality-adjusted productivity gains.

pts.k: The authors are optimistic about future productivity gains as adoption spreads and organizations develop complementary capabilities, without specifying a date or magnitude.
pts.d: Their forward-looking position rests on historical analogies to general-purpose technologies: benefits can take time to emerge while firms redesign workflows, train workers and accumulate complementary assets. They expect global savings to exceed US savings because adoption has already spread internationally. This is an explicitly optimistic outlook rather than a quantified forecast. The paper provides no direct prediction for legal services and no timetable for occupational replacement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Experienced developers capture nearly all measured output and exploration gains despite newer users employing AI more intensively.
pts.d: The authors report approximately 37% AI use among newly joined GitHub users versus 27% among the most experienced. Their heterogeneity models classify developers with at least six years of GitHub activity as experienced, using platform tenure as a proxy rather than directly measuring professional skill. At 29% AI use, experienced users have an estimated 6.2% increase in commit rates; inexperienced users show no statistically significant effect. The authors interpret the concentration of benefits as widening the skill gap, not closing it. They do not directly measure wage inequality or entry-level job displacement. They also report no significant gender difference in adoption among US developers, using name-inferred gender rather than self-identified gender.

pts.k: The authors predict that cheaper code benefits consumers, while effects on programmers' returns depend on market adjustment.
pts.d: In the authors' market scenarios, higher productivity lowers code prices and increases demand. Consumers gain from lower prices and additional consumption. Where the coder workforce is fixed, suppliers gain from greater output but lose from lower prices, leaving their net surplus ambiguous. The perfectly elastic supply scenario assigns gains to consumers without reducing producer surplus, which the authors identify as an extreme assumption. Their own productivity estimates yield illustrative total welfare gains of $21–126 billion under different assumptions. These are conditional predictions, not observed evidence of falling wages or employment.
